task: Write one sentence of your own using the word replete. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know replete should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: At low tide the pools at Cutler Point are replete with hermit crabs — three to a stone, brawling over shells.
A stocked pantry has what the week requires; a replete one is supplied past any counting of the week's needs.
Bursting outdoes replete — the seams themselves complain; nothing more will go in.

Brimming means filled to the very lip of its container, about to spill over — a mug, a stadium, eyes brimming with tears. Replete never sits at a brink; it says richly, thoroughly supplied, often far past need, and it almost always travels with 'with': replete with quilts, with trophies, with proof.

Teeming means swarming with living, moving plenty — a pond teems with tadpoles, a station teems with commuters. Replete cares nothing for motion: a silent archive can be replete with letters. If the plenty crawls and jostles, the scene is teeming; if it is simply richly stocked, it is replete.

Replete means full, abundant.
Great-aunt Lil's attic turned out to be replete with her unfinished projects: quilts folded into cedar chests, coffee cans of buttons sorted by shade, four dresses still pinned to their tissue paper.
We went up for one lamp and came down two hours later, carrying inheritance in armfuls.
Replete is the right word because the attic wasn't merely occupied — it was richly, thoroughly stocked, supplied past any need.
Full reports a level, the way a gas gauge does; replete reports wealth of contents, and it usually travels with with: replete with quilts, with buttons, with the makings of a hundred afternoons.
Replete is the connoisseur's 'full': richly stocked, and nearly always followed by with.
Copious, its unit-mate, counts what pours forth (copious tears, copious notes); replete describes the vessel those things fill — a memoir replete with escapes, a shelf replete with trophies.

For rural families in 1900, the arrival of the mail-order catalog was the shopping trip of the season.
The book ran past a thousand pages and was replete with nearly everything a household could name: plows and pianos, eyeglasses and overcoats, doorknobs, fiddles, and entire kits for building a house.
A farm family forty miles from the nearest town could page through more goods in an evening than a city shopper would see in a month of errands.
Historians treat surviving copies as portraits of an era, precisely because so little was left out.
